name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 20 April 1968

clue.text: It's tenant got booked

blocks.note: surface reading: some tenant of a house got reserved, or charged by the police
setter's reading: the house whose tenant gave a novel its title, so its tenant went into a book

explanation.surface: Somebody's lodger has been arrested or written up.
explanation.walkthrough: Anne Brontë's novel is The Tenant of Wildfell Hall, so the house's tenant was literally put into a book.
explanation.definitionFit: The Brontë novel names its heroine only as the tenant of this house, so the house is the place whose occupant became a book title.

clue.text: World movements?

blocks.note: surface reading: global political or social movements
setter's reading: the idiom asking how the world goes along, as in 'so the world goes'

explanation.walkthrough: The old phrase is 'that's how the world WAGS', meaning how things go on; WAGS is the verb, the world's movement.
explanation.definitionFit: To wag is an old verb for to move along or go on, used in the idiom about how the world goes.

clue.text: How to pack a Gladstone bag?

definitions.text: How to pack a Gladstone bag?

blocks.clueFragment: How to pack a Gladstone bag?
blocks.note: surface reading: advice on filling a kind of hinged travelling bag
setter's reading: the bag is named after the Victorian prime minister who led the Liberal Party

explanation.surface: A packing tip for a Victorian leather travelling bag.
explanation.walkthrough: Gladstone was the Liberal Party leader, so his bag should be packed LIBERALLY, which also means generously, filling it well.
explanation.definitionFit: Done generously and in plenty, which is how you fill a bag; and in a manner fit for a Liberal statesman.

clue.text: "The poet's eye, in a fine rolling" (M. N. Dream)

definitions.text: "The poet's eye, in a fine rolling" (M. N. Dream)

blocks.clueFragment: "The poet's eye, in a fine rolling"
blocks.note: a line from Shakespeare with one word left out between 'fine' and 'rolling'
the source: A Midsummer Night's Dream, Theseus's speech on the lunatic, the lover and the poet

explanation.walkthrough: Theseus says 'The poet's eye, in a fine FRENZY rolling'; the solver supplies the missing word of the quotation.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare pictures inspiration as a wild excitement, a fit of madness shared by lovers, lunatics and poets in the play.

clue.text: Royal turnspit with a predilection for cake

definitions.text: Royal turnspit with a predilection for cake

blocks.note: a pretender to the throne who ended up working the spit in the royal kitchen
his surname is also the name of a rich fruit cake eaten at Easter

explanation.surface: A palace kitchen boy with a sweet tooth.
explanation.walkthrough: Lambert Simnel claimed the English crown in 1487; Henry VII pardoned him and set him to turn the spit. Simnel cake is a British Easter fruit cake.
explanation.definitionFit: The first name of the boy pretender who became a kitchen servant to Henry VII and shares his surname with a festive cake.

clue.text: She made an important pick-up in Othello

definitions.text: She made an important pick-up in Othello

blocks.note: surface reading: a woman made a significant romantic conquest
setter's reading: in the play, a woman picks up the dropped handkerchief that dooms Desdemona

explanation.surface: A woman scored a key romantic catch in Shakespeare's tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: Iago's wife Emilia finds Desdemona's handkerchief and hands it to Iago, setting up the tragedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Iago's wife is the character who retrieves the fatal handkerchief, the object on which the whole plot of jealousy turns.

clue.text: Where Little Buttercup plied her trade?

definitions.text: Where Little Buttercup plied her trade?

blocks.note: the bumboat woman of Gilbert and Sullivan's HMS Pinafore, who sold goods to sailors
setter's reading: she worked among the ship's crew, and the young officers are midshipmen

explanation.surface: A question about where an operetta's market woman did business.
explanation.walkthrough: MIDSHIPS is the middle of a ship; the joke is that she traded aboard ship among the crew, midshipmen included.
explanation.definitionFit: The central part of a vessel, where a trader coming aboard from a small boat would set out her wares to the crew.

clue.text: Liberal has a rendezvous with a caterpillar

blocks.note: L is the standard abbreviation for Liberal
A as written, then RV, the abbreviation for rendezvous
'with' joins on the letter A

explanation.surface: A politician keeps a date with an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: A caterpillar is the immature feeding stage of a butterfly or moth, the classic example of that grub form.

clue.text: Making a verbal approach at the tee?

blocks.note: first sense: speaking to someone, delivering words to them
golf sense: taking your stance and lining up the club behind the ball before striking

explanation.surface: A golfer chatting to the ball before teeing off.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf you 'address' the ball when you set up to hit it, so a golfer at the tee is doing this without saying a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking to someone formally, and the golfing term for setting the club behind the ball ready to swing.

clue.text: Blocks an account for wine

blocks.note: bars are blocks, as of gold or chocolate
AC is the abbreviation for account

explanation.surface: Someone freezes a bank account so they can buy wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Barsac is a sweet white dessert wine from the Bordeaux region of France, close to Sauternes.

clue.text: Sailor with a broken leg goes to the wall in the end

indicators.note: a broken limb is out of shape, so the letters of the limb are rearranged
the sailor is carried within the other word, held in its company

blocks.note: AB, able seaman, is the usual crossword sailor
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: An injured sailor is ruined in the end, going to the wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes to the wall' is an idiom for failing, which hides that 'the wall in the end' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A gable is the triangular upper part of a building's end wall, under the slope of the roof.

clue.text: Followed the winding river

blocks.note: surface reading: walked along the bank of a twisting stream
setter's reading: the Maeander, a famously twisting river in Turkey, gave its name to the verb for wandering

explanation.walkthrough: The verb comes from the Maeander, an ancient river of Asia Minor, so wandering about is literally following that river.
explanation.definitionFit: To wander aimlessly or twist about is named after the ancient river whose bends became proverbial.

clue.text: Heaters for metal workers

blocks.note: first meaning: metal pans or stands holding burning coals
second meaning: workers in brass

explanation.surface: Stoves supplied to keep foundry men warm.
explanation.definitionFit: Coal-burning pans for warmth, and also craftsmen who make articles of brass.

clue.text: He gets a welcome from tug - of - war supporters

blocks.note: taken as written
ave is Latin for hail, a greeting

explanation.surface: A man is greeted by the fans of a rope-pulling team.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the shout heard from people backing a tug-of-war team, urging them to pull.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectators at a rope-pulling contest yell this word to urge their team to pull hard together.

clue.text: Irish landlords?

blocks.note: surface reading: owners of estates let to tenants in Ireland
setter's reading: keepers of pubs, specifically illicit Irish drinking dens

explanation.walkthrough: A shebeen is an unlicensed Irish bar; its keeper is a landlord in the pub sense, not the property sense.
explanation.definitionFit: People who run an unlicensed drinking house in Ireland, the publican sense of the word landlord.

clue.text: See 1 ac
Soupmakers' adequate reserves?

blocks.note: surface reading: hoards built up for future use
setter's reading: cooks need broth base, and plenty of it, in heaps

explanation.surface: Soup kitchens laying in enough supplies.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as STOCK PILES: soup is made from stock, and piles of it are a soupmaker's ample reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: Accumulated reserves of goods held for later use, read here as heaps of soup base.

clue.text: Millinery caused its prosodic change

blocks.note: the hat trade, whose French name is la mode or modes
a short poem's form altered by adding the first letter of millinery

explanation.walkthrough: Put the M of millinery in front of ODE, a poem, and it becomes MODE, fashion in hats: the poem is changed by the hat trade.
explanation.definitionFit: A lyric poem, the prosodic form that turns into the word for fashion when an M is put before it.

clue.text: Hardy but luke warm was Miss Power

definitions.text: Hardy but luke warm was Miss Power

blocks.note: Thomas Hardy, whose 1881 novel is titled after its heroine
Paula Power, the heroine, is lukewarm in religion, like the church of a Biblical city

explanation.surface: A tough woman was nonetheless half-hearted.
explanation.walkthrough: Hardy wrote A Laodicean, about Paula Power; Revelation condemns the church at Laodicea as neither hot nor cold.
explanation.definitionFit: A person indifferent or half-hearted in religion, after the Biblical church rebuked for being neither hot nor cold.

clue.text: Twinkletoes and Dean Farrar's boy get together in secret

indicators.note: twinkling feet dance about, so the word for feet inside this nickname is moved around

blocks.note: the nickname's last four letters, the word for the feet that twinkle
Dean Farrar wrote the Victorian school story Eric, or Little by Little

explanation.surface: A nimble dancer and a cleric's schoolboy meet in private.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twinkletoes' reads as a nickname, but it splits into the instruction and the word to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Understood only by a small inner circle, so private or hidden from outsiders.

clue.text: Not every garcon displays it, however!

definitions.text: Not every garcon displays it, however!

blocks.note: surface reading: not every waiter shows some quality
setter's reading: garçon is French for boy, and you'd expect every boy to show a young lad's character

explanation.walkthrough: A garçon is a French waiter but literally a boy; the 'however!' teases that not every boy is youthfully lively.
explanation.definitionFit: The quality of being like a young lad, which you might expect in all lads but do not always find.

clue.text: Not one smallest coin - that's very bad

blocks.note: no as a negative
the cent is the smallest coin of many currencies

explanation.surface: Being left without a single penny is a dreadful state.
explanation.definitionFit: Nocent is an archaic word for harmful or guilty, the opposite of innocent.

clue.text: Philosopher emerges from a Zion spa

indicators.note: the name comes out of the following letters reshaped rather than as they stand

blocks.note: the letters of these two words, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A thinker steps out of a health resort in Jerusalem.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits nicely: the Dutch Jewish thinker coming out of a spa in Zion.
explanation.definitionFit: Baruch Spinoza was a seventeenth-century Dutch rationalist philosopher of Portuguese Jewish descent.

clue.text: "We have given our hearts away, a sordid --!" (Wordsworth)

definitions.text: "We have given our hearts away, a sordid --!" (Wordsworth)

blocks.clueFragment: "We have given our hearts away, a sordid --!"
blocks.note: a line from a sonnet with its final word left out
the source: the sonnet 'The world is too much with us'

explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's sonnet runs 'We have given our hearts away, a sordid boon!'; the solver supplies the missing last word.
explanation.definitionFit: Wordsworth means a gift or favour: people have traded their hearts for a mean, worldly benefit.

clue.text: In this wise, Browning's soul smoothed itself out

definitions.text: In this wise, Browning's soul smoothed itself out

blocks.note: a phrase from Browning's poem By the Fire-Side
like this: the solver supplies the image the poet compares the soul to

explanation.walkthrough: Browning writes that the soul 'smoothed itself out, a long-cramped scroll freshening and fluttering in the wind'.
explanation.definitionFit: A roll of paper or parchment that, once unrolled, lies flat; the poet's image for a soul opening up.

clue.text: What a figure to cut!

blocks.note: surface reading: what an impression someone makes
setter's reading: a skater cuts a figure into the ice, and one classic shape is two linked loops

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut a figure' means look impressive, but skaters literally cut figures on the ice; the figure of two loops is the number shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A figure is also a numeral, and skaters trace the double-loop number shape as a set figure on the ice.

clue.text: Hungry nestling is an easy catch!

blocks.note: first meaning: a baby bird that stares open-beaked waiting for food
second meaning: in cricket, a simple catch offered to a fielder

explanation.surface: A starving baby bird is easy prey for a predator.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket slang a gaper is an easy chance, a dolly catch.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone or something that opens its mouth wide, as a young bird does, and cricket slang for a simple chance.

clue.text: One double leads to another

blocks.note: surface reading: one double measure of drink follows another
setter's reading: a double chin, so one chin and then another; also a drinking toast

explanation.walkthrough: Chin-chin is a toast said over drinks, and doubled chins give the word its form: one drinking session leads to another.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheerful toast said when raising a glass, and literally two chins in a row.

clue.text: Prize-winning horses

blocks.note: first meaning: laurel wreaths awarded as honours
second meaning: reddish-brown horses with black manes

explanation.surface: Racehorses that have won their events.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition is loose: it is the reward for prize-winning, the bay leaves of a victor's wreath.
explanation.definitionFit: Laurel crowns given to victors, as in winning one's laurels, and the brown colour of certain horses.

clue.text: Poet's near to hope's language

blocks.note: the letters of these words, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A poet is close to finding the language of hope.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no anagram signal; the fodder has exactly the right letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The invented international language takes its name from its creator's pen name, meaning one who hopes.

clue.text: That's the end of the letters

definitions.text: That's the end of the letters

blocks.clueFragment: That's the end of the letters
blocks.note: surface reading: the correspondence is over
setter's reading: the final character of the Greek alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: The letters are the Greek alphabet, which ends with its long o.
explanation.definitionFit: The twenty-fourth and last character of the Greek alphabet, hence a byword for the finish of anything.

clue.text: Would a rod from this tree make you smart?

blocks.note: surface padding: a cane cut from the tree would make you sting, adding a pun on the second meaning
first meaning: a coniferous evergreen
second meaning: neat and well turned out

explanation.surface: Would a cane cut from this wood make you sting?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart' looks like the sting of a beating with a rod; it is the adjective meaning neat.
explanation.definitionFit: A conifer of the pine family, and also an adjective for being trim and well groomed.

clue.text: Dashing lovers irritate hill-dwellers

blocks.note: to gall is to vex or irritate
ants live in anthills

explanation.surface: Swaggering suitors annoy the locals of the hills.
explanation.definitionFit: Gallants are stylish, attentive men who court women, fashionable wooers of an older age.
